problem_text: Let G be a finite group and L a maximal subgroup of G. Suppose L is non-Abelian and simple. Then there exist at most two minimal normal subgroups in G.
solution_text:
Proof: Assume for contradiction that G has three distinct minimal normal subgroups N1, N2, N3.

Step 1 (Dichotomy): For each Ni, since L is maximal and Ni ◁ G, either Ni ≤ L or G = NiL. If Ni ≤ L, then Ni ◁ L (as Ni ◁ G), so Ni = L (since L is simple and Ni ≠ {e}). At most one Ni can equal L.

Case 1: L is not normal in G (no Ni equals L).
Then all Ni satisfy Ni ∩ L = {e} and G = NiL, giving |Ni| = |G|/|L|.
For N1, N2: [N1, N2] ≤ N1 ∩ N2 = {e} (distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize each other). N1N2 ∩ L ◁ L, so N1N2 ∩ L = {e} or L. If {e}, then |N1N2L| = |N1||N2||L| > |G|, contradiction. So G = N1N2 and |N2| = |L|.
For N3: N3 ≤ G = N1 × N2 (direct product). N3 centralizes N1 and N2, so N3 ≤ Z(N1) × Z(N2).
Now |N1| = |L| and L is non-abelian simple. By Burnside's p^a q^b theorem, |L| is not a prime power. Since N1 is a minimal normal subgroup with |N1| = |L| not a prime power, N1 cannot be elementary abelian. So N1 is non-abelian, hence Z(N1) = {e}. Similarly Z(N2) = {e}.
Therefore N3 ≤ {e}, contradiction.

Case 2: L is normal in G (some Ni = L, say N1 = L).
G/L is simple (L maximal). For Nj (j≥2) with Nj ≰ L: Nj ∩ L = {e}, |Nj| = |G/L|.
If G/L ≅ Z/p: |Nj| = p. If N2, N3 both exist: N2N3 ∩ L ◁ L is non-trivial (by counting) and proper (|N2N3 ∩ L| = p < |L|), contradicting L simple.
If G/L is non-abelian simple: |Nj| = |G/L| not a prime power, so Nj is non-abelian and Z(Nj) = {e}. If N2, N3 both exist: N3 ≤ Z(N2) × Z(L) = {e} × {e} = {e}, contradiction.

In all cases, at most 2 minimal normal subgroups exist.
solution_summary: The proof uses a dichotomy from maximality (each minimal normal subgroup N either lies in L, forcing N=L, or satisfies N∩L={e} and G=NL), then splits into two cases. When L is not normal in G, all minimal normal subgroups have |N|=|L|, and Burnside's theorem (|L| not a prime power) forces them to be non-abelian with trivial center, trapping any third one in {e}. When L is normal in G, at most one N equals L and at most one N is outside L (two outside would create a non-trivial proper normal subgroup of L, contradicting simplicity).
answer: G has at most two minimal normal subgroups, i.e., the number of minimal normal subgroups of G is ≤ 2

rounds.expected_answer: We have a finite group G with a maximal subgroup L that is non-abelian and simple. We need to prove G has at most 2 minimal normal subgroups. This is a structural bound theorem in finite group theory.

rounds.question: List all relevant facts and tools about maximal subgroups, minimal normal subgroups, and simple groups that might help bound the number of minimal normal subgroups.
rounds.expected_answer: Key facts: (1) Minimal normal subgroups are characteristically simple (products of isomorphic simple groups). (2) Distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize each other: [N1,N2] ≤ N1∩N2 = {e}. (3) If L is maximal and N◁G, then either N≤L or G=NL. (4) L simple means any normal subgroup of L is trivial or L itself. (5) Burnside's p^a q^b theorem: non-abelian simple groups have order divisible by at least 3 primes, so |L| is not a prime power.

rounds.question: Try a direct approach: assume three minimal normal subgroups N1, N2, N3 exist and try to derive a contradiction using just the definitions and the maximality of L.
rounds.expected_answer: If N1, N2, N3 are distinct minimal normal subgroups, they pairwise centralize each other. For each Ni, since L is maximal, either Ni ≤ L or G = NiL. If Ni ≤ L, then Ni ◁ L, so Ni = L (since L is simple). At most one can equal L. For the others, Ni ∩ L = {e} and G = NiL. But I'm stuck on how to get a contradiction from three such subgroups.

rounds.question: For the case where N ∩ L = {e} and G = NL, compute |N| in terms of |G| and |L|. Then for two such N1, N2, determine the structure of G = N1N2 and what constraint this puts on a third N3.
rounds.expected_answer: |N| = |G|/|L| since N ∩ L = {e} and G = NL. For two such N1, N2: they centralize each other, so N1N2 = N1 × N2. Also N1N2 ∩ L ◁ L (since N1N2 ◁ G), so N1N2 ∩ L = {e} or L. If {e}, then |N1N2L| = |N1||N2||L| > |G|, contradiction. So N1N2 ∩ L = L, meaning G = N1N2 and |N2| = |L|.

rounds.question: Now for a third minimal normal subgroup N3: since G = N1N2 and N3 ◁ G, where must N3 live? Use the centralization property of distinct minimal normal subgroups.
rounds.expected_answer: N3 ≤ G = N1N2 = N1 × N₂ (direct product since they centralize each other). Since N3 centralizes both N1 and N2 (distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize each other), N3 ≤ Z(N1) × Z(N2). So we need to determine Z(N1) and Z(N2).

rounds.question: What is |N1|? Is N1 abelian or non-abelian? Use Burnside's p^a q^b theorem to determine this, and then determine Z(N1).
rounds.expected_answer: |N1| = |L| (from the counting argument). L is non-abelian simple, so by Burnside's p^a q^b theorem, |L| is divisible by at least 3 distinct primes, hence |L| is not a prime power. Since N1 is a minimal normal subgroup with |N1| = |L| not a prime power, N1 cannot be elementary abelian (which would have prime power order). So N1 is non-abelian, hence N1 is a product of non-abelian simple groups, and Z(N1) = {e}. Similarly Z(N2) = {e}. Therefore N3 ≤ {e}, contradiction.

rounds.question: We've handled the case L ≁ G. Now handle the case L ◁ G (when some Ni = L) and conclude the proof.
rounds.expected_answer: If L ◁ G: at most one minimal normal subgroup equals L. For any other N ≰ L: N ∩ L = {e}, |N| = |G/L|, and G/L is simple (L maximal). If G/L ≅ Z/p: two such N2, N3 would give N2N3 ∩ L ◁ L non-trivial and proper, contradicting L simple. If G/L non-abelian simple: same Burnside + center argument. So at most one N ≰ L. Total: at most 2 minimal normal subgroups. QED.
